In 4 of its 5 New Testament uses (80%) the Majority Standard Bible renders it "swindlers," listing such people alongside other wrongdoers, while the one outlier (Matthew 7:15) uses the predatory image of false prophets who are inwardly ravenous beneath their sheep's clothing. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes that Deissmann found the word current as a Latin loan-word in comedy, and argues that in Paul it is better translated "swindler" than "robber" — pointing to a financial, fraud-related flavor rather than violent theft.
prose.caution: The single Septuagint occurrence (Genesis 49:27) and the lone Matthew use show the word also carried a more violent, predatory sense, so its range spans both fraud and rapacity.

prose.def: A down payment or deposit given in advance that guarantees the full amount will follow later.
prose.article: ἀῤῥαβών is a commercial term for a first installment handed over as security that the rest of a payment will come — what older Bibles called an "earnest." The Majority Standard Bible renders all 3 New Testament occurrences as "pledge," and the BSB agrees fully. The word is Semitic in origin, mirroring the Hebrew עֲרָבוֹן, and shows up in everyday business papyri — one document records a woman receiving 1,000 drachmae as a deposit for a cow; remarkably, in Modern Greek the word came to mean an engagement ring.

prose.def: Describing words or things that cannot or may not be spoken, whether impossible to express or too sacred to repeat.
prose.article: This word combines a negative prefix with the idea of "spoken," so it means something not uttered — either because it can't be put into words or because it's too sacred to say aloud. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 12:4, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it simply as "things" (the phrase "inexpressible words"). The most telling evidence comes from the papyri and inscriptions, where Moulton-Milligan shows the word was tied to the secret "mysteries" of ancient religion — for instance a 61 BC inscription from Mantinea speaks of guarding the unspoken mysteries of a god — which fits Paul's sense of words too holy to repeat.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and a low confidence tier, the precise force here — "impossible to express" versus "forbidden to speak" — rests heavily on outside inscriptional evidence.

prose.def: An adverb meaning right now, at this very moment, marking the strictly present time in contrast to past or future.
prose.article: ἄρτι pins down the immediate present — "just now," "at this very moment" — as opposed to what came before or what is yet to come. The Majority Standard Bible renders it "now" in 19 of its 36 New Testament appearances (63%), with a handful of cases where it shades into "still" or simply gets folded into the surrounding phrasing. The everyday papyri make its flavor vivid: one writer says he can't come to you "right now" (ἄρτι) because of a lawsuit, and a rescript of Hadrian uses it of a city that was "just" incorporated. Abbott-Smith notes it contrasts with both past and future time and stands close in meaning to νῦν.
prose.caution: With only two Septuagint occurrences, the Old Greek evidence is thin, so its range there rests almost entirely on New Testament and papyri usage.

prose.def: A chief or ruling angel, the highest rank among angels.
prose.article: ἀρχάγγελος combines the ideas of "ruler" (ἄρχω) and "angel" (ἄγγελος) to mean a chief or superior angel. Strikingly, Moulton-Milligan notes it is older than once thought: an Eleusis inscription from around 300 B.C. uses it of "sound, white, unspotted" stones, showing its everyday literal sense.

prose.def: A venomous snake, specifically the asp or cobra, often associated with deadly poison.
prose.article: In the New Testament ἀσπίς refers to a venomous snake — the asp or cobra. It appears only once, in Romans 3:13, where the Majority Standard Bible's measured rendering counts toward "graves" but the word itself names the snake whose poison is under deceitful lips. In the Septuagint it shows up 20 times across 8 books, most often translating the Hebrew פָּ֫תֶן (pethen, a venomous serpent). Interestingly, the same Greek word can also mean a round shield, and the Rosetta Stone (196 BC) uses ἀσπίς of the asp adorning the king's golden crowns.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its New Testament range rests on a single verse and on Septuagint evidence.

prose.def: Refusing to make peace; unwilling to be reconciled or bound by any truce.
prose.article: The word literally points to someone "without a libation" — the drink-offering that once sealed a treaty — and so describes a person who will not be reconciled or bound by any peace agreement. It appears only twice in the Byzantine New Testament (in Romans 1:31 and 2 Timothy 3:3), rendered "faithless" and "without" in the Majority Standard Bible, where it sits among lists of hardened, broken character traits. The most telling outside evidence comes from Priene, where the phrase "asylei kai aspondei" turns up seven times meaning "without formal treaty"; Moulton-Milligan neatly captures the metaphor for 2 Timothy as "friends need no treaty, and implacable foes will not make one."

prose.def: A small, low-value Roman copper coin, worth a fraction of a day's wage.

prose.def: Describing someone as beautiful, fine, or attractive in appearance.
prose.article: In the New Testament ἀστεῖος appears just twice, both times meaning "beautiful" — once of the infant Moses in Acts 7:20 and again of him in Hebrews 11:23. The word originally meant "belonging to the city" (from ἄστυ, a city), and like the Latin urbanus it could carry shades of "refined," "elegant," or "courteous," but that civic connection had faded in everyday Koine. A striking bit of evidence comes from the papyri, where a document from around 245 BC uses it of fine clothing — "let him wear as fine clothes as possible."

prose.def: Not in agreement or harmony; describing people whose views clash or sounds that don't blend.
